name: Adriel
title: Merab's husband from Mehola
summary: Adriel, son of Barzillai the Meholathite, took Merab to be his wife – King Saul’s eldest daughter – after the king broke his promise to give her to David. The marriage likely had a political dimension in Saul’s strategy to weaken David’s influence. However, Adriel’s name is most closely associated with the tragic event that unfolded during David’s reign: A prolonged famine was attributed to Saul’s breach of covenant against the Gibeonites, and as atonement, David handed over seven of Saul’s descendants – among them the five sons Merab had borne to Adriel. This account raises profound questions about inherited guilt, the unyielding nature of covenants, and how the actions of kings could impact future generations in Israelite society.
roles: Father of five sons who were handed over to the Gibeonites

keyEvents.title: Saul promises Merab to David
keyEvents.description: King Saul promised his eldest daughter Merab to David as a wife after David had distinguished himself in battle against the Philistines. However, Saul had ulterior motives and hoped that the Philistines would take David's life in combat.

keyEvents.title: Merab marries Adriel
keyEvents.description: Contrary to his promise to David, Saul gave his daughter Merab to Adriel, son of Barzillai the Meholathite. This breach of covenant was part of Saul's ongoing attempts to undermine David's position and influence.

keyEvents.title: The Gibeonites' demand for atonement
keyEvents.description: During a three-year famine, David sought the Lord and learned that the cause was Saul's bloodguilt against the Gibeonites. The Gibeonites demanded that seven of Saul's descendants be handed over to them to make atonement.

keyEvents.title: Adriel's Five Sons Executed
keyEvents.description: David handed over the five sons that Merab had borne to Adriel, along with Rizpah's two sons, to the Gibeonites. The seven were executed on the mountain in the presence of the Lord at the beginning of the barley harvest.

keyEvents.title: Rizpah's Vigil and the Burial
keyEvents.description: After the execution, Rizpah, mother of two of the slain, faithfully kept watch over all seven bodies to protect them from birds of prey and wild animals. Her steadfast devotion moved King David, who gathered the bones of the executed together with those of Saul and Jonathan and ensured a dignified burial in Kish's family tomb.

The marriage was likely motivated by political considerations in Saul’s effort to marginalize David. Adriel’s fate is inextricably linked to a tragic event during David’s reign: When a prolonged famine struck the land, the Gibeonites demanded atonement for Saul’s mistreatment of them. footnotes.text: In 2 Sam 21:8, the Masoretic text reads "Mikal" instead of "Merab" as the mother of Adriel's five sons. Most textual scholars consider this a scribal error, since 1 Sam 18:19 clearly states that Merab was given to Adriel. Mikal was married to Paltiel (1 Sam 25:44). Several ancient manuscripts and translations correct it to "Merab".

Adriel's father Barzillai is called the "Meholathite," linking the family to Abel-meholah in the Jordan Valley. This is the same place from which the prophet Elisha came (1 Kgs 19:16). The city was likely located in the northern part of the Jordan Valley, a fertile agricultural region.

The Gibeonites' demand for blood vengeance (2 Sam 21:1–9) reflects an ancient Semitic legal concept of collective guilt and vicarious atonement. Saul's breaking of the covenant with the Gibeonites (Josh 9:15–27), according to the narrative, had consequences that extended beyond his own generation.

The name Adriel (Hebrew: עַדְרִיאֵל) likely means "God's flock" or "God's herd," composed of עֵדֶר (eder, "flock/herd") and אֵל (El, "God"). The name may reflect a pastoral background and fits with the family living in the fertile agricultural land of the Jordan Valley.

Barzillai, Adriel's father, should not be confused with the much better-known Barzillai from Gilead who helped David during Absalom's rebellion (2 Sam 17:27; 19:31–39). The title "the Meholathite" clearly distinguishes him from the Gileadite Barzillai.

The execution of Adriel's sons took place at the beginning of the barley harvest (2 Sam 21:9). This timing may have had ritual significance in an agricultural context, where atonement was symbolically linked to the land's fertility and God's blessing over the crops.
